en: Now begins the chapter on words.
Now, having established rejoicing through mindfulness as a cause, we shall here explain this means of valid cognition, verbal testimony, which stands between those two.
The cognition of that object produced by the speech of an untrustworthy person is not a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa),
because no defect in its cause or any sublation is observed; nor is the speech of an untrustworthy person itself a valid means of knowledge.

Because of the observation of defects in the cause and the presence of sublation, there is no sublation by means of [the reasons] such as "being a sentence," for that would involve a contradiction with one's own words.
If the statement presenting the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) is not in accordance with reality, then how can there be subversion?
Or, if it is in accordance with reality, [then what?]
If that [instance] were also included within the subject (pakṣa), it would be contradicted by that very [reason];
if it were excluded from the subject, there would be an inconclusive reason (anaikāntya) due to that same instance.
Nor does this lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
For it is impossible to deny that sentences such as those spoken by the deluded are rooted in defects, whereas in this case (the Veda) such defects are absent.

Furthermore, although things like words carved by woodworms or those produced in a dream have the capacity to convey meaning, they are not to be trusted because they lack any specific intended purpose (*viśiṣṭatātparya*).
And because deviation is observed;
for even in the eternal Veda, which consists of the eternal command of God, there is no loss of its intended meaning regarding this or that specific purpose,
whereas such [intended meaning] is absent here [in the case of the opponent's position].
Furthermore, the observation of occasional defects is no different in the case of perception and other means of knowledge;
and whether validity is intrinsic or extrinsic, there is no distinction between them in that regard.
Nyāyabindu, Pariccheda 1, Śloka 6: Furthermore, with respect to the objective aspect (vedyāṃśa), that [cognition] is distinct from direct perception because it lacks immediacy,
like inference.
It is distinct from inference,
because the consideration of the subject (pakṣa) and the logical mark (liṅga), and so forth, are not observed [in its case];
and because words, sentences, their relations, and so on, are not logical marks with respect to the specific meaning of a sentence, since they lack established pervasion (vyāpti).
Because there is no distinction in all cases once the acceptance of an example is granted,
and because the capacity to convey meaning is established as being independent even in the case of linguistic usage;
for this very reason, the authority of the word (śabda) is established even when one accepts the inference of the speaker's cognition.
If it is argued that "cognition based on scripture is inference, because it is a means of valid cognition other than perception, like [any] commonly accepted [inference]," we say no.
Because this has already been answered;
otherwise, cognitions of sound, taste, smell, and so forth would be inference,
because they are cognitions not produced by the eye.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that [the opponent] would be like one who has already accepted [the point].
"Direct perception, inference, and scripture consisting of various traditions— "

Furthermore, the distinction between verbal testimony and inference is observed from the consensus of great sages such as Manu, who stated that [knowledge] "is born from perception, inference, and scripture.
Nor can the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (gobalīvarda) be applied here,
for no subsumption [of one under the other] is seen.
If it is argued that scripture is inference because it brings about cognition only when a relation has been grasped, we say no;
for there is a rule that the nature of inference requires the apprehension of a relation distinct from the relationship between the object to be known and the means of knowing.
Nor is there here any relation distinct from those [two],
the apprehension of which would necessarily have to be required;
otherwise, because of the dependence on a relation, it would be easy to prove that those two are themselves perceptible.
Nor is it memory, because its object is something previously unknown. A sentence is a specific collection of words.
A "word" (pada) is that which is the object of the linguistic usage of authoritative persons.
Its manifestation is brought about even by the conceptualization of it as ending in a nominal suffix (sup) or a verbal suffix (tiṅ), and so forth.
For this very reason, the bases (prakṛti), suffixes (pratyaya), and so on, are conceptualized differently in various grammatical systems.
And that [nature] is not conventional,
because a person who could establish the convention is impossible;
for this very reason, its establishment is not like that of other languages.
And because they are eternally contained within the Vedas;

for those very words that are Vedic are also worldly, as established by such statements as, "In the beginning, [words] arose from the Vedic sounds alone. However, regarding the difference between colloquial speech (*bhāṣā*) and Vedic meter (*chandas*), there is a distinction in the grammatical rules (*lakṣaṇa*) for certain words, which depends upon their respective specific sequences (*ānupūrvī*).
Every word employed in common speech is found used somewhere in the Veda;
however, the established rule is that certain words are restricted exclusively to the Veda and do not occur elsewhere.
And this has also been stated in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*: "All words that are expressive are indeed Vedic," and so forth.
Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Śabdapariccheda 3: A sentence is of two kinds, distinguished as human (pauruṣeya) and non-human (apauruṣeya).
That which is characterized by a specific arrangement dependent upon human independence is human.
It is of two types: that whose meaning is connected [to other words] and that whose meaning is not connected.
The first is, for example: "Fire is hot; water is liquid.
The second is, for example: "Fire is not hot."
Water is solid.

In this regard (Nyāyapariśiṣṭa, Śabdanirūpaṇa 4), the proponents of a partial view (ekadeśin) say: "The conventional usage of related meanings arises in some cases due to the non-perception of the lack of relation (ananvaya).

For this very reason, in the case of worldly sentences, because deviation is observed, there is no immediate determination of the sentence-meaning from the sentence itself; rather, it requires the consideration of semantic competency (yogyatā) and expectancy (sākāṅkṣatva)."

Even when the fitness for the universal is apprehended, the fitness for the individual is not established without the inference of the speaker’s cognition—this has been demonstrated in the *Prameyasaṃgraha* and other works.

Likewise, in the context of the objection that the scripture would become a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*) because it would refute perception as apprehending only the existent (*sanmātra*), the author of the *Vivaraṇa* stated: "The intention is that it is a defect for a word, whose natural function is to inform what is unknown, to be otherwise."
Alternatively, [the word] would merely be reiterative (*anuvādaka*). For a word is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding an object already cognized through another means of knowledge;

for its linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) is established in that very way. Having said this, and having established the inference of the speaker’s cognition by means of the passage beginning with, “But surely, in the case of human statements, linguistic competency is established precisely through reiteration,” he says: “True, ...”
"By virtue of divine providence, its status as a restatement [of what is already known] does not entail a violation of the natural aptitude for awakening the unawakened;

just as, even though the Veda inferred from Smṛti is a restatement, its authority is not undermined because of its underlying purpose. And so it is said in the *Prajñāparitrāṇa*: "The words of human authors, seized by doubt, do not immediately produce valid cognition..."
They do not produce [it] as long as there is no restraint of the pride that takes them as its root.
And having inferred that other valid cognition which is the source of the speaker's [utterance] and is appropriate as its basis,
they infer the meaning of the sentence by means of the sign (liṅga) of the sentence spoken by him.
This sentence is always fit for expressing a connected meaning;
furthermore, he does not speak untruth, so he spoke that for the sake of providing a designation.
Through the inference of the speaker’s cognition, based on one's own words being known or unknown,
there arises from speech a cognition of the mere capacity for expressing connected meanings.
What is termed "apprehension" (parāmarśa) does not have the connection between objects as its domain;
rather, compatibility (yogyatā) is defined as the state of not being contradicted by other means of valid cognition.

Now, if a worldly sentence is a logical mark (liṅga) because it possesses the characteristics of a logical mark, then— since the word [of the Veda] has its relationship [with the object] already grasped— it too must possess the status of a logical mark in that same way.
At the time of learning [a word], the learner has no cognition of a logical mark (liṅga) because there is no doubt;
for it is only words as they have been learned that convey meaning. If this is argued, then:
Since the cognition of the object would arise from itself alone, it cannot function as a logical mark (liṅga).
And so forth.
However, by the venerable Yāmunamuni, the inference of the speaker’s knowledge was refuted regarding the authority of scripture (*āgama*),
and he concluded as follows:
"Therefore, in cases such as 'there is fruit on the riverbank,' that cognition which has an established object is verbal, not inferential. This very position was adopted by Varadaviṣṇumiśra.
This has also been explained in detail in the *Tattvaratnākara*, following the citation of the section on the authority of scripture (*āgama-prāmāṇya*).

All non-human (apauruṣeya) [Vedic] utterances indeed possess connected meanings; however, in cases such as "The sacrificial post is the sun" (*ādityo yūpaḥ*), the consistency is maintained through figurative usage (*upacāra*).
For words that possess expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*) denote a connected meaning.
Alternatively, they rest upon the secondary meaning;
for there is an abandonment of the primary function due to the incompatibility between the words *āditya* and *yūpa*, whose distinct literal meanings are established by direct perception.
Nyāyapañjikā, Śabda section 5: Function (*vṛtti*) is twofold, distinguished as primary denotation (*abhidhā*) and metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).
Primary denotation is the function that consists in the very meaning established by etymology;
for example, the word "lion" [denotes] the king of beasts.

That [secondary function] is of many kinds, due to differences in the objects such as genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*), and due to the distinctions between etymological derivation (*yoga*), conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), and their combination.
Metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) is the operation [of a word] upon something proximate to its primary meaning when that primary meaning is obstructed.
And this proximity is twofold: connection with the primary meaning and connection with its qualities.
Among these, the first is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by way of the primary meaning (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇā*),

as in the case of "A hamlet dwells on the Gaṅgā," where the word "Gaṅgā" refers to the bank, which is related to its denoted object— the specific flow of water. In this same manner, indication by indication (*lakṣita-lakṣaṇā*) is to be understood.
By the second [type of usage], the application is figurative (*gauṇī*).
For example, in the expression "Devadatta is a lion," the word "lion" applies to Devadatta because he possesses qualities such as courage.
In the *Tattvaratnākara*, however, it is stated thus: "Therefore, the relationship of signifier and signified is established between the word and its object."
In this context, the expression of the relationship should be understood as twofold: primary and secondary.
For one who intends to employ a word for the purpose of understanding the meaning expressed by it,
that [cognition] which has the power of the word as its cause is called "primary" (mukhya) with respect to its own object.
"By means of expressing its own primary meaning, it is considered to have a secondary meaning in another sense.
Thus [it is said].
The detailed exposition of that should be sought in that very same place.
Nor is there a lack of denotability for metaphorical (gauṇa) and indicative (lākṣaṇika) usages simply because their objects are not directly denotable;
for even though they function solely through relation or similarity, they are beginningless.
Precisely for that reason, usage is established as appropriate in the intended instances according to the requirements of each case.
All these modes of operation (*vṛtti*) are included within the mode of denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*).
Individual words merely serve as reminders;

for if one were to accept the theory of "denotation of the related" (*abhihitānvaya*), there would be the unnecessary burden of postulating three powers: a power in the words to denote word-meanings, a power in the word-meanings to convey the sentence-meaning, and a power in the words to convey that [sentence-meaning].
Otherwise, it would follow that the meaning of the sentence is not verbal (*aśābda*);
furthermore, since the definition [of a word] is completed with respect to the word-meaning (*padārtha*), it would follow that [the sentence-meaning] lacks a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nor is there a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) in the theory of the expression of related meanings (*anvitābhidhāna*).
This is because it subsists merely on mutual recollection.

As they have said: "The entire collection of words, when heard, recalls their respective meanings which are not yet connected; subsequently, its manifestation brought about by logical reasoning (nyāya) leads to the cognition of the sentence-meaning."
Thus.
Nor is there the fault of tautology and so forth,
because each part has a power restricted to its respective portion;
nor is there a split in the sentence.

Because they denote their own meanings by virtue of having a single predominant sense, it has been stated: "The meaning of the sentence is indeed the meaning of the word-constituents, for it is the [meanings] in conjunction that are denoted.

Likewise, in the section beginning with "Due to the difference in words and so forth" (*nānā śabdādibhedāt*), although words such as "one should know" (*veda*) and "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*) denote the repetition of the mental act (*pratyaya*), [they do not differ in their essential nature].
"And although the cognitions have Brahman as their sole object,

nevertheless, the knowledge consisting of the repetition of those cognitions— which brings about the realization through the repetition of cognitions whose objects are Brahman qualified by attributes such as being the sole cause of the universe and being free from sin, as declared in their respective contexts— distinguishes [Brahman]."

In the *Vedārthasaṃgraha* as well, it is stated: “Even among the purificatory [passages], such as ‘Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite’ and ‘Brahman is bliss,’ it is not contradictory that they denote a single entity qualified by multiple attributes established through the grammatical principle of apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); thus, Brahman itself, qualified by all [attributes], is what is denoted.”

In this very same earlier section, it is stated: "Immediately upon hearing a sentence—which consists of a collection of words that denote related meanings—one understands that what is conveyed by one word is indeed fit for connection with what is denoted by the other words uttered alongside it;
and that [meaning] takes the form of being a means to attain heaven."

Therefore, the principle that "an action must not have another purpose" has been abandoned precisely because of the contradiction [with the observed facts]. This natural inclination belongs to the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of related meanings). Furthermore, there is no evidence here to suggest that this was stated merely by accepting the opponent's position.

Varadaviṣṇumiśra also, in many passages such as "And because the theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna) is untenable if words like 'truth' and 'knowledge' have the meaning of a single undivided essence," has directed his critique against the proponent of Māyā precisely at the doctrine of anvitābhidhāna.
And it is stated in the *Āgamaprāmāṇya*: "Even if the expression of the related to something else [is accepted], the practical usage [of language] is established."
This quality of expressing a connected meaning must necessarily be resorted to.
Beginning with these words, [it continues]:

"Therefore, all proponents of philosophical views must accept that the derivation of word-meanings occurs in relation to their own referents as connected with other meanings that are required, proximate, and capable."
Thus, in the *Tattvaratnākara* as well: "The denotation of related meanings must necessarily be resorted to;
thus the teachers of Yāmunācārya have declared the theory of the denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) by means of words themselves."

Having begun with these words and established the position through an elaborate argument, [the author] concludes: “Since the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of related meanings) is here supported by six arguments beginning with common experience—arguments that have shaken off all objections—the theory of *abhihitānvaya* (the relation of expressed meanings) is not established by means of words; thus, everything is consistent when viewed from the opposite perspective.”
Thus.
And it has been stated many times in both the *Prajñāparitrāṇa* and the *Nyāyasudarśana*: "The capacity of a word to denote a connected meaning is based on its inherent power;
the opposite [non-denotation] arises from a defect in the person's intellect regarding the understanding [of that power] acquired through linguistic usage."
By such [passages] as these.
Surely there also exist sentences that indicate the connection of already-expressed meanings (*abhihitānvaya*).

In the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*, for instance, it is stated: "In this way, where the sequence of utterance of those collections of words—which are denoted by the term 'sentence'—which cause understanding by making known a particular relation [between meanings], is preceded by human intelligence... and so forth.

Likewise, in that very same [work] it says: "Because a word, consisting of stem and suffix, contains within it multiple qualifiers, whereas a sentence conveys the connection between the meanings of multiple words.
And in the Bhāṣya as well: "But a word, in particular, possesses the capacity to denote an object only as qualified."
This is because [language] functions in the form of words and sentences.
For a word-status arises through the conjunction of a stem (*prakṛti*) and an affix (*pratyaya*);
and due to the distinct meanings of the stem and the affix, it is inevitable that the word itself conveys a specific, qualified meaning.

It has been stated [in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*] that "the differentiation of words is based on the differentiation of meanings," because a sentence, which consists of a collection of words, expresses the specific relations between multiple word-meanings.

Thus, in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*, while defining linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*), it begins: "The apprehension of a word’s power to convey meaning regarding established entities (*siddhavastu*) is extremely easy."

Having explained the manner of incidental acquisition of meaning through the sentence "The staff is in the room," and having likewise established the grasping of the expressive power (*śakti*) of individual words toward their respective referents through deliberate instruction— such as by saying to a child, "This is a cow" (*gaur ayam*), "This is a horse" (*aśvo ’yam*), and so forth—
Furthermore, after stating, "This meaning belongs to this word; thus he was instructed by the elders of old," and so forth, it is further said:
"In this very way, he understands that all words denote their own individual meanings, and that specific combinations [of words] denote specific relations as they actually exist."

In the *Bhāṣya* as well, while refuting the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the first sūtra, the derivation of word-meanings (*padavyutpatti*) was previously established by means of such statements as: “In this way, indeed, worldly people determine the relationship between words and their meanings—[for instance] through mothers, fathers, and others, [they learn] ‘mother,’ ‘grandfather,’ ‘uncle,’ and so forth.
And therein it was stated: “They ascertain that the employment of those words with respect to those respective objects is based upon their capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatva*).”
Furthermore, [the text says]: "Regarding words that are both conventional and non-conventional, he has been taught by the elders of old that 'this is the meaning of this word,'" and so forth.
If indeed the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of the related) is intended, then how could there be any linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) regarding individual words alone?
And if that were the case,
how could the denoted meaning be connected [to the word], since it would entail the consequence of a reversal in linguistic convention?
Therefore, some maintain that it cannot be determined that the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) alone is the final established conclusion.

Others, however, maintain that the statement beginning with "of those who inform" (*bodhakānām*) is appropriate because the specific relation (*saṃsargaviśeṣa*) is established within the related whole (*anvite*).
Furthermore, the mention of the distinction between words and sentences is intended merely to demonstrate the specific qualifications of each, or to indicate the positions accepted by others.
The explanation of the etymology of each individual word is merely the illumination of a unique means conducive to the cognition of the connected meaning.
For it has been stated that words cause the understanding of the sentence-meaning only after they have caused the recollection of the word-meanings.
And since recollection is rooted in one's own prior experience, there is no need to postulate a further capacity [of the words].
And Śrī Rāmamiśra has explained the Bhāṣya and other works in his *Vivaraṇa* as being intent upon [the meaning of] connection (*anvita*).

Likewise, in the *Ṣaḍarthasaṃkṣepa*: "A word, by its own nature, causes that which is capable [of being expressed] to be understood as connected; it does not [denote] another meaning because of impossibility."
For thus has it been stated: "This is indeed the etymological derivation," and so forth.
Therefore, the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the denotation of the related) is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In this way, both by the power of *anvitābhidhāna* and because the cognition of the qualified [meaning] would otherwise be impossible, it is established that words themselves denote the qualified [meaning].
For this very reason, the claim that even though [a word] denotes a qualified object (*viśiṣṭārtha*), its power (*śakti*) resides only in the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is also refuted;
for there is no other power apart from the capacity to denote.

Furthermore, the argument regarding "non-termination" (*aparyavasāna*) is untenable, because that which has the power to bring about the cognition of a qualified object cannot rest upon the qualifier alone.
For a qualifier that has entered into what is qualified merely serves as a further embellishment; thus, such a form is difficult to apprehend without the apprehension of the qualified object.

And since the apprehension of the qualified object is for that very purpose, the statement [that it is apprehended first] is useless, because it is only logical to establish things according to how they are perceived.

Furthermore: If the cognition of the individual were to arise from the very nature of the object—such as "cowness"—denoted by words like "cow," then it would likewise occur in the case of abstracting terms as well.
However, words such as "cow" express universals and the like as dependent [upon individuals].

If it is argued that the substratum is understood by that [word], then our desired goal is established. But how can there be a cognition of dependence without first making the other [the substratum] known? If it is made known, would the word not then possess a power (*śakti*) with respect to that [dependence]?

The awakening of another by means of the dependent nature through the Buddha is likewise [untenable]; if the dependent nature were awakened by that [Buddha’s] cognition, there would be mutual dependence. If the state of being dependent is understood as being independent of another cognition, [then it is not truly dependent].
By that [extraction], there would not be the cognition of another [property], just as in the case of an extracted [conceptual] apprehension.
If its own nature were dependence on another, then that [dependence] would be equal even in the case of the extractor;
we perceive nothing else [as a distinguishing factor] beyond the fact that it is grounded in the locus (dharmin).
The theories concerning *nirūḍha-lakṣaṇā* (established metaphorical indication) apply to words whose cognition is independent of reference to other words and which function as synonyms.

This is because, in the case of the word "cow" (*gauḥ*), there is no extraction [of the universal] from the individual; however, if such extraction were to occur, it would depend on a prior [cognition].

Furthermore, because it is not observed in the case of abstracting terms (*niṣkarṣaka*), there is no indication of the individual (*vyakti*) by means of the genus (*jāti*). Why does he who considers the power of words to reside in the configuration (*ākṛti*) alone not accept that it resides in existence (*sattā*) itself for all of them?
Therefore, one must necessarily admit that the cognition of a specific object arising from words such as "cow" is produced by the power of the word itself.
As for what was stated by Śrī Rāmamiśra in the *Ṣaḍarthasaṃkṣepa*— namely, "There is no loss of worldly linguistic convention, because the expressive power (śakti) resides in that very [convention]"—
that too is intended merely to refute the absence of expressive power in that regard.
However, for one whose intellect is incomplete, there arises the delusion that the Vedānta has not been heard;
for it is stated immediately thereafter that its completion occurs through study based on superficial understanding (*āpātavyutpatti*).

And as it says in the *Ātmasiddhi*: "Just as the word-potency (*padaśakti*) of words such as 'cow' relates to the universal aspect, even though the object consists of both the universal and the particular as established by a single cognition."
Furthermore, that example accepted by the opponent is intended for another purpose;
this is because of the use of "just as" (*yathā*) to provide an illustration acknowledged by the opponent,
and because even in a word expressing a quality (*guṇa*), the principle stated for class-words (*jātiśabda*) applies.
Because it denotes that which is inseparably established [with its substrate], a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) of the possessor of qualities (guṇin) is not tenable.

When the mantra arising from specific vowels and genders is omitted, there is no consecration (saṃskriyā). Furthermore, we do not consider that it expresses a qualified entity when it lacks its own inherent meaning.

Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Śabdanirūpaṇa, Section 9: Therefore, since there is a linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) whereby words other than those that denote by extraction (*niṣkarṣaka-śabda*)—namely, those denoting inseparably established qualifiers (*apṛthaksiddha-viśeṣaṇa*)—terminate in their respective substrata (*viśeṣya*), it is established that even words such as "deity" (*deva*), which denote bodies, terminate in the embodied being (*śarīrin*) according to their usage.
For this very reason, words such as "self" (*ātman*) and "earth" (*pṛthivī*) terminate in the Lord (*īśvara*).

Therefore, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in such passages as "All this is Brahman," "The luminaries are Viṣṇu," "This self is Brahman," and "That thou art," refers to Brahman as qualified by those respective modes.
Furthermore, the manifestation of names and forms (nāmarūpavyākaraṇa) occurs through its entry [into them].
For this very reason, it is also heard in scripture that He is denotable by all words.
And that very point is manifested by the text: "Having entered into that, it became both the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat).
It is also recorded in the Smṛti: "You pervade everything; therefore, You are everything.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "But the designation [of Brahman] as dependent on the moving and the non-moving would be figurative, because [Brahman] exists when those [entities] exist."
And it has been said by Varadaviṣṇumiśra: "By the word *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven), a person who desires heaven is denoted.
For the Lord, having attained all desires, does not desire heaven, because [to him] it is a very slight pleasure."
Therefore, there is figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) regarding the individual soul (jīva), which is a single part of the literal meaning, just as the word "Ganges" [indicates] the riverbank.
Alternatively, even words such as "one desiring heaven" have their primary meaning (mukhyatva) in the individual soul alone.
Because the basis for the application [of the term] is not abandoned;
for this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that even a figurative word (*bhākta-pada*) functions as a designation by way of metaphor (*bhaktyā*).
If it is asked: "Since a specific form is the object of the primary denotative power (*śakti*), why is there not a case of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) when that [form] is connected [to the meaning]?"

This is because the established rule is that "primary" status consists in denoting only that which has entered into the etymological derivation without abandoning its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), whereas "metaphorical" usage is caused by the absence of that [basis].

Nyāyapañcāśikā, Chapter 10: Now, an objection is raised: in the statement "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*), if "thou" (*tvam*) refers exclusively to Śvetaketu, then its grammatical coordination with "that" (*tat*) is untenable.
If "thou" refers to the Lord residing within Śvetaketu’s body, then it is impossible to instruct [the disciple] by facing him directly as that [Lord].

Furthermore, prescribing the meaning of "thou" with reference to that [Lord] is utterly rejected on the grounds that it would result in a lack of syntactic connection with the word "art" (*asi*), and so forth.
Even though the conclusion (*nigamana*) consists of restating what has already been established, the distinction between the qualifier and the qualified must still be extracted [from it].
Likewise, designations such as "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*) are also difficult to justify.

Furthermore, in the phrase "by means of the living self" (*jīvenātmanā*), the use of the word "self" (*ātman*) to denote the individual soul (*jīvātman*) contradicts the statements of the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*).
This is because of the designation "by me through the living self" (*jīvena mayā*) and so forth; however,
if the Supreme Self were intended, the use of the instrumental case would be untenable,
since [the agent] has already been expressed by the verb "I shall manifest" (*vyākaravāṇi*).

Even though there is a difference in action, because the subsequent action of the act of making (*kṛti*) is uniform, it is illogical for there to be another agent, as this would contradict the requirement of a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*).
If one intends to express the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) [of the act], then using the third case (*tṛtīyā*) for the agent results in a loss of its primary status.
Therefore, just as one might enter an enemy force through a spy and take command, so too does the individual soul (jīva) possess agency upon entering [the body];
whereas the Supreme Lord is merely the agent of its manifestation.
However, by that much alone, it is not established that words have that [Supreme Lord] as their ultimate referent.

Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Śataślokī, verse 11. To this it is replied: First of all, the awakening (*saṃbuddhi*) here is accomplished solely through the instruction on the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyopadeśa*) directed at Śvetaketu alone; thus, there is no addressing of one who is not to be awakened.
Furthermore, the explicit form of the statement is precisely "That thou art" (*tad asi*).
In that regard, by way of the relationship between cause and effect, [the identity is established].
Alternatively, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) may be maintained by treating the body as the self;
in either case, it is established that the word "you" (*tvam*) also terminates in the substance denoted by the word "that" (*tat*).
When one property is qualified by another property, there is non-difference from itself;
this constitutes identity between the material cause and that which possesses it.

Therefore, when the intention is to express that Brahman has you as its body (*tvaccharīrakaṃ brahma*), the mere designation "you" (*tvaṃ*) and "that" (*tat*) is appropriate; furthermore, the use of the second person pronoun is based on the employment of the word "you" (*tvaṃśabda*), because of the grammatical rule: "When *yuṣmad* is used as a co-referential term (*samānādhikaraṇa*), even if it remains unexpressed (*sthānin*), the second person [verb] is employed."

Therefore, that [word "tat"] also terminates in the same referential object as the word "thou" (*tvam*). Alternatively, let the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) be simply "That art thou" (*tat tvam asi*).
Nor is there a rule that the verbal suffix (*tiṅ-vibhakti*) must conform to the subject (*uddeśya*).

Since there is no contradiction here either—just as in the case of the specification of gender, number, and so forth that conforms to what is to be adopted (upādeya)—Patañjali and others employ even a verbal suffix (tiṅ-vibhakti) that conforms to what is to be adopted, as in such passages as: "That same lump of gold, when returned, becomes two earrings with the color of khadira-wood embers," and so on.
By this, the statement "I am Brahman" and others are also established.

In the phrase "by the living self" (*jīvenātmanā*), by this same reasoning, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word *jīva* with the word *ātman*—which is a synonym for the word *sva* (self)—is established.

However, the impossibility of the instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is equally applicable whether one holds the view of identity of essence (*svarūpatādātmya*) or the view of distinctness (*pṛthaktva*).

If, however, one seeks some way to resolve this by distinguishing [the self] through its different aspects (*aṃśabheda*) and so forth, with the intention of expressing its status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) and the like, [then it may be justified].

Likewise, you should accept that even here [in the case of Brahman], the explanation is achieved by distinguishing [the terms] through the intention to express differences such as specific forms and so forth.

Therefore, in statements from the Śruti and other sources, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) which is accompanied by contradictory meanings does not have its locus solely in identity of essential nature.
The cognition of grammatical coreferentiality arises from [the relationship of] being an effect, non-separability, entering [into], imitation, existence, creation, assistance, and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that in such passages as "All this is indeed the Person" (Puruṣa-sūkta) and "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is intended for the purpose of sublation— just as in the case of "The man [seen] is a post"—

because such [sublation] is impossible when the primary sense of the words is applicable, and because the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and so forth is established by the force of uncontradicted perception and other means of knowledge.
However, grammatical coreferentiality with the aspect of consciousness (*cidaṃśa*) cannot withstand sublation,
because you yourself also admit its reality;
furthermore, if identity of essential nature were established, it would be obstructed by contradictory attributes.

If that [secondary sense] were abandoned, there would be the consequence of the co-referentiality of synonymous terms, since the word "pada" would have no meaning distinct from it; furthermore, in the absence of a [primary] means, the sublation of the primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*) would result; and since another possible interpretation exists, such [sublation] is improper.
Furthermore, if there were a mere indication of the essential nature [of the word], other words would be redundant;
moreover, the difference in the essential natures [of words] is established by many means of valid cognition.
Nyāyapariśuddhi, Chapter 1, Section 12: Even a definitional statement such as "Truth, Knowledge... has a single object qualified by [attributes] such as truth;
for grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is understood in precisely that way.
Nor does it follow here that a difference in the substratum arises from a difference in the qualifiers.
Because there is an absence of contradictory qualifications;
for there is no contradiction here as there is between a jar and a cloth, etc.
And just as in the case of perception, there is no contradiction between blueness and being a lotus due to the force of direct observation, [so it is here].
The same applies here as well;
nor is any rule of non-co-referentiality observed regarding truth, knowledge, and so forth,
such that there would be a contradiction.

However, when grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is intended to signify the identity of the qualificands, the mutual difference between the qualifiers and between the qualifiers and the qualificand is indeed an advantage.

Nor does there follow from this the consequence of the identity of the qualifiers with each other, or the identity of the qualifiers with the qualificand, in the same way that the identity of the qualificands [with one another] follows.
Because of defects such as contradiction with the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, and because there is no conventional understanding (*vyutpatti*) to that effect;
nor is there the defect of mutual inherence (*samavāya*) and so forth among the qualifiers, due to the prescription of another qualifier within the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*).

Because it expresses a single qualified entity simultaneously with its many qualifiers, and because even in cases of injunctions following a restatement, the primary focus remains on the property (dharma) according to established linguistic usage.
Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Śabdapariccheda 13: Nor is every qualifier incapable of coexisting with another qualifier, because it is only opposed to its direct opposite;

otherwise, due to contradiction with perception, there would follow the impossibility of the arising of inference and other means of knowledge whose objects are qualified by properties such as those that prove or are to be proven.
In this way, even conventional usage such as "this does not indicate a distinction" would be abolished;
yet it is not so in the case of verbal expression or communication,
because there is no such lack of distinction there.
Since an object must be made known by verbal testimony just as it is by perception and other means of knowledge,
it is not even admitted that [the word] refers solely to the qualifier; for if that were the case, the identity of the qualified entity would remain unestablished.
However, for one who holds that [the word] refers solely to the substantive (viśeṣya),

there would be defects such as synonymy, the futility of other words, and the loss of the defining characteristic; this is because the qualifiers, which serve as the grounds for the application [of the term], would be abandoned.
Furthermore, since the mere qualificand, being devoid of a means of access, cannot be the object of definition;

and whether the exclusions of others (*itaravyāvṛtti*) are taken as accidental characteristics (*upalakṣaṇa*) or as the essential nature (*svarūpa*), the same fault of the redundancy of other words and so forth remains.

Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Śabdakhaṇḍa 14: Thus, if these [qualities] function as qualifiers, then the defects you mentioned—such as the distinction of the qualified (*viśiṣṭabheda*) and so forth—would apply just as they do in other alternative positions; if they do not apply there, then they do not apply here either. To desire the exclusion of that which is contradictory to it while having abandoned the basis for its application is like desiring to dispel darkness after having discarded the light.
A sentence that appears contradictory [in its literal sense] has an indivisible ultimate meaning,
because it is a sentence of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*),
like the sentence "This is that Devadatta."
Or if it is argued that this is because it is a defining statement (lakṣaṇavākya), like "The moon is the most excellent light," we say no,
because the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) is unestablished.
For it is precisely Devadatta, as qualified by having had teeth and now having them fallen out, that is recognized in the cognition "this is he.
If it is argued that there is a contradiction between those two states occurring simultaneously, we say no,
because simultaneity is not what is being asserted.
And because there is no [logical] entailment;
moreover, simultaneous apprehension is not a fault,
for otherwise, if recognition were undermined, doctrines such as momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and selflessness (*nairātmya*) would be defeated.
If it is asked, "Even so, how can both pastness and presentness belong to one and the same thing?
[the answer is: For at the time of its own destruction, it would indeed be past by itself, yet it has not been destroyed.
Because it is perceived as being present;
for its reality consists in its connection with a specific past limiting condition (*upādhi*), and not in its state of having passed away.
If it is asked, "How can one [entity] be both prior and posterior?", we say no, because both are possible through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that serve as constraints;
otherwise, even a moment (*kṣaṇa*) existing between prior, posterior, and middle would be subject to the fallacy of being further divisible.
For it is not the case that it possesses priority even over what precedes it, nor posteriority even over what follows it.
If it is argued that "let it perish moment by moment," we say no.
Because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of the negation of everything;
let this matter rest— nevertheless,
even the second example refers only to that which is qualified.
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence that the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) could not arise,
and the qualifiers such as "excellence" (*prakṛṣṭatva*) and so forth would be rendered meaningless.
In this same manner, the sublation of the two inferences by scripture (*śruti*) must also be stated.

There is also a counter-argument characterized by the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of [the sentence] being synonymous and so forth. Thus, a sentence that is subject to dispute is qualified as having a supreme referent,
because it is a sentence endowed with expectancy (ākāṅkṣā).
Like a sentence with discordant grammatical cases,
this inferential reasoning (anumāna) that serves as a sublation is also more powerful, owing to its conformity with actual cognition and the establishment of its corroborative instance (dṛṣṭānta).
Grammarians themselves have stated that "co-referentiality" (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is the occurrence of words with different grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) upon a single object.
In this definition, the phrase "with different grounds for application" serves to exclude synonyms;
the word "single" is for the purpose of excluding those that are non-co-referential, such as "pot" and "cloth," as well as those that are not syntactically connected.

The phrase "in the meaning of words" (*śabdānām arthe*) is intended solely for the sake of clarification; or rather, it is for the purpose of indicating that the "meaning" (*arthe*)—as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)—is the primary object denoted.

Consequently, even though in sentences with different grammatical subjects (*vyadhikaraṇavākya*) there may be the possibility of a function directed toward a single primary referent, that [referent] is excluded because it lacks the status of being the qualificand.
The operation of making known the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is here called both *vṛtti* and *pravṛtti*, both generally and specifically;
for *pravṛtti* is indeed an excellent (*pra-kṛṣṭa*) *vṛtti*,
and excellence here consists in having the qualificand as its object.
In this context, that which serves as the condition (upādhi) for the application of a word to its qualificand is the ground for its application (pravṛttinimitta).
It is thus stated that grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) consists in the denotation of a single qualificand by means of distinct qualifiers.

[Objection: Now, it was established that all human speech possesses a connected meaning; however, that is not tenable, because such a quality is observed only in sentences composed by a speaker who possesses excellence (*guṇavat*).
If this is argued, it is not so,
because of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*); for, by its own nature, every cognition is seen to produce uncontradicted practical activity (*avyāhata-vyavahāra*).
For the status of being a cause for the conventional usage of "sublated" in certain cases is conditioned by specific adjuncts such as the non-apprehension of difference.
Consequently, even though validity is intrinsic, it is in some instances set aside by an obstructing defect (*doṣa*),
just as the heat of fire [may be obscured].
In that case, validity exists solely in relation to that portion [of the object];
however, the excellences (guṇas) serve only to eliminate defects in instances where defects might be suspected,
since there is no pervasion (vyāpti) of validity by them.
For those who maintain that [the Buddha] is eternally omniscient, there is a deviation in his cognition when it has become a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
However, the fact that invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is dependent upon defects (*doṣa*) is established by an invariable positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
If it is objected: "How can invalidity, which is a non-entity (*avastu*), be something to be produced by a cause?", we say: no.
This is because that [negation], in the form of doubt, error, and so forth, lacks the status of being a non-entity (*avastu*); furthermore,

we do not admit the existence of a negation that is distinct from a positive entity (*bhāva*), and even if such were admitted, we observe that destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) is produced by hammers and other such causes.
In the same way, valid cognition (*pramā*) also arises from something distinct that is common to both correct and false awareness,
because it is a specific kind of effect,
like invalid cognition (*apramā*); thus, validity is known extrinsically (*parataḥ*).
If it is argued that [the cognition] is non-authoritative because it is characterized by doubt during the state of non-habituation, just like [any other] lack of authority;
In that regard, if the first position takes "all valid cognition" as the subject (*pakṣa*), the reason is partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddhi*) according to our own view,
because we accept that God's valid cognition is eternal.
If the position takes "valid cognition other than God's" as the subject, then the qualification is useless until God has been established.
If it is argued that the formal syllogism (prayoga) follows immediately after the inference for God (īśvarānumāna), we say no;
for that [inference] cannot be established through reasoning, according to the principle of the section on the scripture as the source of knowledge (śāstrayonyadhikaraṇa).
If it is then argued that we shall not employ the qualification [of the subject], we say no.

If it is argued: "Because [the reason] is inconclusive due to the cognition of an Īśvara as accepted by oneself; for what would be the rebuttal when Buddhists and others who do not accept an Īśvara employ such an argument?"—we say no, because it is possible to state either a sublation (*bādha*) or an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) by means of establishing that eternal valid cognition is proven by scripture (*śruti*).
If it were the case that the qualification "being an effect" would be fruitful by way of excluding the eternal validity established by scripture (*śruti*),
then how could its establishment through scripture occur without first determining the authority of that scripture?
And if its authority is accepted on the grounds of its being eternal and faultless, [then the objection remains].
How, then, can there be the production of validity from another in that case?
For it is your established tenet that the validity of sentences depends upon the qualities of the speaker;
and the quality [in question] is simply the state of being free from defects.
If it is argued that, because [validity] depends upon that [external factor], validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*) in that case, we say no;
for our opponents do not admit that the absence of an obstructing factor is a cause [of cognition].
And even if they were admitted, there would be no contradiction with the Veda’s being authorless and eternal, since [validity] would depend on that much alone.
For indeed, your undertaking to establish extrinsic validity (*parataḥ prāmāṇya*) is for the purpose of proving that the Veda has an author and so forth;
whereas we demonstrate intrinsic validity (*svataḥ prāmāṇya*) precisely for the purpose of proving that it is authorless and so forth.

Now, if it is maintained that—given the establishment of the Veda’s authority through its being the word of a reliable person (*āpta*), which in turn establishes the existence of God—a qualification is required to exclude that [divine] cognition, [we reply:]...
That too is not the case;
for if validity were established extrinsically, you would then establish that its validity is rooted in an authoritative person, and upon that being established, God would be established.

The qualification is for the purpose of excluding that [other] cognition; however, if this reason, being thus qualified, were to establish extrinsic validity (*parataḥ prāmāṇya*), it would result in the fallacy of circular reasoning (*cakraka*).

In order to avoid the charge of being otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhi*) regarding the inference for God (*īśvarānumāna*), the extrinsic nature of validity (*parataḥ prāmāṇya*) is demonstrated in the *Nyāyakusumāñjali*;
and it is precisely there that the qualification "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is employed.
Now, a qualification is not logically appropriate merely for the purpose of excluding unestablishedness (*asiddhi*).

However, if the validity [of knowledge] is established as extrinsic (*parataḥ*), then the effort to prove that [extrinsic validity] does not serve that purpose [of establishing intrinsic validity], and thus it remains difficult to overcome. Even so, if it is argued that the validity of verbal testimony depends upon the qualities of the speaker, we say no, because there is no distinguishing factor [to differentiate the two cases].
And because there is a requirement for that [corroboration] in cases where defects are suspected, whereas the Veda is free from defects;
if it is argued that extrinsic validity (*parataḥ prāmāṇyam*) is thereby established since [validity] depends on the absence of defects— no, [it is not].
Because there is no dependence upon that [other],
since it consists merely in the cessation of contradiction;
or, let there be such dependence.
Nevertheless, there is no fault in the case of the Veda.
If it is argued that the absence of defects cannot occur without the presence of excellences, we reply that this is not so,
because we observe the cessation of both [heat and cold] in the case of a touch that is neither hot nor cold.
And because it is logically consistent:

if it is argued that for one who maintains that non-existence is a distinct entity, the absence of faults is itself a merit, we say no, because that [non-existence] is established by means of another intrinsic non-existence.
For even in that case, the absence of cold is not necessarily heat itself,
because it is unestablished as such in that which is neither hot nor cold;
rather, its nature as the absence of cold consists in the inclusion of both states.

Likewise, in this case as well, the absence of defects is common both to the words of authoritative persons who possess qualities and to the Vedic statements which are devoid of a speaker's qualities.
Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Śabdanirūpaṇa, Section 16: Now, if words were intrinsically valid (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), would not even the statements of the Buddha and others be intrinsically valid?
They would not; for intrinsic validity is a general rule (*utsarga*), and it does not apply to specific cases where there is a contradiction.
And it is stated in the *Āgamaprāmāṇya*: "In the case of verbal testimony, there are no defects inherent in the word itself that obstruct its validity;
rather, its status as a means of valid cognition is intrinsic—such is the established position."
In some cases, [the meaning] is set aside due to a defect in the speaker's intention,
as in such statements as, "A herd of elephants is on the tip of a finger," and so forth.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore: "In the case of the eternal Veda, there is no dependence on the qualities of a cause, just as in the case of the cognition of God.
If you argue that there is no fault here because of the absence of a cause, then for us, it is the same here because of the absence of a speaker."
Just as knowledge attains the status of being valid without an external cause,
so too a sentence is, by its own nature, the cause of valid cognition.
If invalidity follows from the absence of excellence in the cause, then this [invalidity] would likewise be unavoidable for you even in the case of God’s valid cognition.

Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Śabdanirūpaṇa, 17: Now, if you argue that—in the absence of both excellence and defect in the cause, since neither validity nor invalidity (which are produced by those two) can possibly exist, and because no other alternative is possible—the cognitions generated by Vedic words would be devoid of any nature;
this [objection] applies equally to the cognition of the Lord (Īśvara).
If it is argued that the cessation of the cause would remove its effect— validity— but not [the validity] that is eternal,
then the same applies to the cessation of the causes of invalidity as well.

Therefore, there would either be a conjunction with contradictory natures, or, through the abandonment of both [possibilities], it would result in a state of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Thus, for those who do not admit a Lord (such as the Buddhists and others), since a dominant cause, a cooperative cause, or the qualities thereof— such as the causal factors in the case of the continuum of pure consciousness (*śuddhasaṃvitsantāna*) and so forth— are impossible, and because they accept that validity has its own inherent scope directed toward itself, these arguments are equal.

Even though the causality of the preceding cognition is accepted, nevertheless, because that [cognition] existing in the state of final liberation (apavarga) stands in opposition to all latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) consisting of qualities, defects, and so forth, it cannot be the cause of a quality produced by it. Furthermore, as for the fact that validity is known extrinsically (*parataḥ*):
Thus it has been stated.
In that case, since it is accepted that one cognition is cognized by another cognition, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).

If the intention is to say "only by another [cognition]," then this is impossible in the case of a cognition that, by its very definition as "this kind of cognition is valid," encompasses all valid cognitions, as well as in the case of the supreme Lord’s omniscient consciousness (*pārameśvara-vijñāna*).
For it is not the case that the truth of those two [cognitions] is not apprehended by themselves,
as that would entail the consequence that their definitions are over-extensive (*ativyāpti*) or that they are merely partially knowledgeable (*kiñcijjñatva*).
If it is argued that there is a rule that in other cases [of cognition], [truth] is established only extrinsically (*parataḥ*);
That too is not correct,
because it can be countered by that very same example: "The validity under dispute is known by its own substratum,
because it has the nature of validity."
[It is] like the validity of the knowledge of Īśvara and so forth.

If it is asked, "In that case, how is there room for doubt as to whether this is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or not?"—if you say this, we reply: no, because we observe the arising of doubt even when things are perceived in their specific details.

Just as one whose intellect is blinded by the delusion of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell repeatedly wonders, even when it is perceived as such, "Is this indeed silver as it is perceived? Or is it, as before, a case of silver in a shell?"—so too here, even though validity is being apprehended, one must consider: does this [cognition] exist as valid and is being perceived as valid?
Or, due to sublation, does it exist as invalid, like a previous error?
Thus, doubt is indeed appropriate.
Nevertheless, if it is argued: "What is the use of the mention of 'one's own' (svataḥ) when one must endure doubt? For certainty itself depends entirely on another," [the response follows].
Can apprehension or non-apprehension be regulated by our own preference?
For it is the established mode of apprehension that must be followed by investigators. If it is asked, "How is this establishment itself [known] intrinsically?"—
In this way— namely, that cognition, while illuminating its own object, also illuminates itself independently of another cognition— is a point agreed upon by all Vedāntins.

Even in the theory that [cognition] is not self-illuminating, the determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*), when appearing through the subsequent reflective cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) which apprehends it, is nonetheless seen to be non-doubtful in nature.

In the *Nyāyapariśiṣṭa*, chapter 18, even in the theory that recollection (*smṛti*) lacks authoritative validity, [this cognition] is distinct from recollection because it has as its object a novel thing (*apūrvārtha*), and it is of the nature of non-erroneousness and non-sublation,
since sublation and the like could not possibly occur prior to it. Consequently,
this determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) first appears with such-and-such an object as its domain.

Because they mutually examine one another precisely by virtue of having that [object] as their domain, even subsequently; therefore, the validity characterized by having that as its domain—which is established later—is already grasped at the very outset. Thus, there is the apprehension of validity intrinsically (*svataḥ*).

Nyāyapariśuddhi, Chapter 1, Section 19: Now, it might be argued that even invalidity characterized as doubt and so forth can be apprehended initially through self-luminosity or through after-cognition (anuvyavasāya);

however, invalidity characterized as error (*viparyayatva*) cannot be so apprehended, because the contrariety of what is being grasped is not apprehended by itself or by its grasper at the first moment.
And since there is no dispute among the Vaidikas regarding that portion,

and since they ultimately proceed to establish the authority [of the Vedas] by taking up that very portion— even from the perspective of the Pasupatas— there is no initial non-authority because of the absence of defects therein.
For this very reason, because the cognition of invalidity is impossible, and because the cognition of validity is established intrinsically and remains uncontradicted, it is so stated.

Thus ends the first Āhnika of the Śabdādhyāya in the Nyāyapariśuddhi, among the works of the illustrious Veṅkaṭanātha, the Vedāntācārya, the lion among poets and logicians, who is independent in all philosophical systems.
